CausalChain: 3D scaffold formation -> Enhanced cell–cell/ECM interactions & robust tight junction formation -> Activation of integrin/FAK signaling -> Temporally decoupled and sequential activation of Wnt/β-catenin and YAP/TAZ pathways -> Targeted epigenetic modifications at CYP gene promoters (increased histone acetylation, decreased DNA methylation) -> Increased CYP expression and improved drug metabolism modeling
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that culturing HepG2 cells within a custom-engineered 3D hydrogel scaffold—with precisely adjustable mechanical properties and defined biochemical ligands—will improve cell–cell and cell–ECM interactions, leading to the formation of robust tight junctions that mimic the architecture of in vivo hepatocytes. This physical reorganization is expected to trigger integrin-mediated FAK signaling, which we propose activates the mechanotransductive pathways Wnt/β-catenin and YAP/TAZ in a temporally resolved and sequential manner. Such activation is anticipated to induce targeted epigenetic reprogramming at CYP gene promoters, as evidenced by increased histone acetylation and decreased DNA methylation, ultimately leading to enhanced CYP expression and more faithful drug metabolism modeling. To rigorously test this hypothesis, we will use a modular experimental design that employs high-resolution time-lapse imaging, CRISPR-based reporter assays, real-time PCR, and ChIP-seq, complemented by selective pharmacological inhibition and ligand-specific scaffold modifications. Additionally, we plan to conduct control experiments decoupling mechanical from biochemical cues and extend the study to include primary hepatocytes, ensuring that the observed effects are not artifacts of the HepG2 model.
Abstract: In this study, we propose that engineering a 3D hydrogel scaffold with precisely tunable mechanical and biochemical properties will not only enhance cell–cell and cell–extracellular matrix (ECM) interactions in HepG2 cultures but also promote the formation of robust tight junctions mimicking in vivo hepatocyte architecture. Importantly, we postulate that this engineered physical microenvironment will initiate integrin-mediated focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signaling, which, in a temporally resolved and partly decoupled manner, sequentially activates the mechanotransductive pathways Wnt/β-catenin and YAP/TAZ. Activation of these pathways is hypothesized to drive targeted epigenetic modifications—specifically, increased histone acetylation and decreased DNA methylation—at cytochrome P450 (CYP) gene promoters. These modifications are expected to enhance CYP expression and thereby improve drug metabolism modeling. Our approach leverages advanced methodologies including high-resolution time-lapse imaging, CRISPR-based reporter assays, ChIP-seq, and selective pathway inhibition, while also incorporating experimental designs to decouple and temporally map the effects of mechanical cues versus biochemical signaling. Furthermore, we propose to extend our findings by validating the model in primary hepatocytes, thereby addressing potential limitations of the HepG2 cell line and reinforcing clinical relevance.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the original causal chain: (1) formation of the 3D scaffold boosts cell–cell/ECM interactions and robust tight junction formation, (2) integrin-mediated FAK signaling is activated, (3) this leads to sequential activation of Wnt/β-catenin and YAP/TAZ pathways, and (4) resulting in epigenetic reprogramming at CYP gene promoters enhancing CYP expression and drug metabolism modeling. However, the new formulation addresses review concerns by: (a) emphasizing a temporally resolved and decoupled activation of the signaling pathways to reflect potential crosstalk and temporal dynamics; (b) incorporating experimental controls to separately determine the contributions of mechanical versus biochemical signals; (c) leveraging contemporary techniques such as CRISPR reporters and high-content imaging for precise temporal mapping; and (d) proposing validation in primary hepatocytes to broaden the model's translational relevance. These enhancements refine the mechanistic clarity and practical implementability of the original hypothesis while maintaining its novelty and logical coherence.
